title: "Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/01-files/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](01-files-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Which kind of file holds the measurements?

Did seedlings grow differently after a nutrient treatment? The measurements are
**simulated teaching data** from 24 seedlings in separate pots, 12 treated and 12
controls, each measured at the start and after seven days; `data/README.md`
describes the study. Before we analyse them we look at the file they are stored
in. Some files are plain text, which any program can read. Others, such as Word
and Excel files, are packages that only particular programs understand, and
spreadsheets can even change the data. No programming today.

## Downloading the course folder

1. Download [the course files](../downloads/course-files.zip).
2. In the browser's downloads list, choose **Show in folder** (Windows) or
   **Show in Finder** (Mac). The file is usually in **Downloads**.
3. **Extract** the ZIP: on Windows, right-click `course-files.zip` and choose
   **Extract All**; on Mac, double-click it.
4. Move the extracted folder `introcomputing-course` into **Documents** and work
   there, never inside the ZIP. It contains the folders `data`, `examples`,
   `output` and `reports`, and the files `report.Rmd` and `introcomputing.Rproj`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## I see two course folders. Which should I use?

Extraction can create an extra outer folder, and downloading twice gives names
ending in `(1)`. Open folders until you find the one that directly contains
`data`, `output` and `introcomputing.Rproj`, and use that one. Ask before
deleting the other.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## My Documents folder is in OneDrive or iCloud

Tell the teacher. A cloud-managed Documents folder can show a file (with a cloud
icon) that is not yet on the laptop, so we check that the course files open
with the network turned off.
:::

The ending of a filename, such as `.csv` or `.docx`, is its **extension**. File
managers often hide it, so turn it on: in Windows File Explorer choose
**View → Show → File name extensions**; in Mac Finder choose
**Finder → Settings → Advanced → Show all filename extensions**.

## A plain-text editor

A **text editor** shows exactly the characters stored in a file, with no
formatting. On Windows, use Notepad: right-click a file and choose
**Open with → Notepad**. On Mac, use TextEdit, set to plain text under
**TextEdit → Settings → New Document → Plain text**. TextEdit tries to display
Word files as documents, so to see what is really inside a file use
**File → Open**, click **Options** and tick **Ignore rich text commands**.
Later in the course, RStudio will be our text editor.

## What is inside seedlings.csv?

Open `data/seedlings.csv` in the text editor to find out how much plant P01
grew. The first lines are:

```text
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
P02,control,24.3,32.3
```

The first line is a **header** that names the columns, and each following line
describes one plant. P01 started at 25.7 mm and ended at 44.3 mm, so it grew
44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. Nothing else is in the file: only letters, digits,
commas and line breaks. Such a file is **plain text**, and a **CSV**
("comma-separated values") file is a table written as plain text. Every editor
shows the same characters, and R can read them directly.

Plain text works for anything that can be written as characters. Open
`data/dna.txt` and you see a DNA sequence of the letters A, C, G and T. The
plain-text files you will meet in this course are:

| Extension | What it holds | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.csv`, `.tsv` | tables (commas or tabs between values) | `data/seedlings.csv` |
| `.txt` | notes, DNA sequences | `data/dna.txt`, `data/field-notes.txt` |
| `.md` | documentation, with simple marks such as `#` for headings | `data/README.md` |
| `.R`, `.Rmd` | R code, and R Markdown reports | `report.Rmd` |

## What is inside a Word file?

The folder `examples` holds the same short note about the experiment as
`seedling-notes.txt` and as `seedling-notes.docx`, saved by a word processor.
Open both in the text editor (not in Word) to find out where the Word file keeps
the text. The `.txt` shows the note; the `.docx` starts with `PK` followed by
unreadable symbols, because a `.docx` file is a compressed **ZIP package**.

To look inside, copy `examples/seedling-notes.docx` into `output`, rename the
copy `seedling-notes.zip` (accept the warning) and extract it. Inside the folder
`word`, open `document.xml` in the text editor. The sentences of the note are
there, surrounded by tags such as `<w:p>` and `<w:t>` that mark paragraphs and
text. The package holds 16 files, among them `styles.xml` with fonts and
headings and `docProps/core.xml` with the author and dates, and Word puts them
together when it opens the document.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## TextEdit shows the formatted note instead of `PK`

Use **File → Open → Options → Ignore rich text commands**. If that does not
help, copy the `.docx` into `output`, rename the copy to end in `.txt`, and open
the copy.
:::

Excel files (`.xlsx`) are packages of the same kind. PDF files and pictures are
not text either: open `examples/seedling-notes.pdf` and
`examples/seedlings-plot.png` in the text editor, and the first characters,
`%PDF` and `PNG`, tell programs which format follows.

## The same table as CSV and as Excel

Open `examples/seedlings.xlsx` in a spreadsheet program (Excel or LibreOffice
Calc) to find out what an Excel file stores beyond the measurements. It holds
the same 24 plants as `data/seedlings.csv`, plus a bold, coloured header row, a
column `growth_mm` whose cells are **formulas** (click E2 and you see `=D2-C2`
while the cell shows 18.6), and a second **sheet** called `notes`.

A CSV file can store none of these: it holds values only, one table per file.
That is why this course keeps data as CSV. Any program can read it, including R
and a text editor, and what the text editor shows is exactly what is stored.
Formatting and calculations belong in R code, where every step is written down;
a coloured cell is information that R never sees.

## Can a spreadsheet change the data?

Open `examples/genes.csv` in the text editor and then in Excel to find out what
Excel does to the gene symbols `SEPT2` and `MARCH1`. Excel guesses that they are
dates and shows `2-Sep` and `1-Mar`. If the file is saved, the gene names are
replaced for good. (LibreOffice usually keeps the names; the lecture slides show
what Excel does.) Ziemann and colleagues (2016) found such errors in about
**one in five** published papers that had gene lists as Excel files, and in 2020
the human gene naming committee (HGNC) renamed these genes, for example to
`SEPTIN2` and `MARCHF1`, partly for this reason. Older data files still use the
old names.

Then open `examples/seedlings-semicolon.csv` in the text editor and compare it
with `data/seedlings.csv`:

```text
plant_id;treatment;initial_mm;final_mm
P01;control;25,7;44,3
```

This is how Excel saves "CSV" on a computer set to Swedish (and many other
European languages): the comma is the decimal sign, so semicolons separate the
values. A program that expects commas splits these rows in the wrong places, so
look at every CSV in a text editor before analysing it.

For this course: if you look at raw data in a spreadsheet, close it **without
saving**.

## Text editor or word processor?

A **word processor** (Word, Pages, Google Docs) is made for formatted documents
and changes what you type. Compare the last line of the two notes from
`examples` to find out what Word did to a line of R code:

```text
seedling-notes.txt:   seedlings <- read.csv("data/seedlings.csv")
seedling-notes.docx:  seedlings <- read.csv(“data/seedlings.csv”)
```

Word replaced the straight quotes `"` with curly quotes `“ ”`. R understands only
straight quotes, so code copied from the Word file stops with
`Error: unexpected input`. Write code, data and notes for analysis in a text
editor, and later in RStudio. TextEdit on Mac is a word processor too unless you
choose **Format → Make Plain Text** before saving; otherwise it saves a
formatted `.rtf` file.

## Renaming and file extensions

Renaming a file changes its name, not its contents. Renaming the `.docx` to
`.zip` worked because the file was a ZIP package all along. Renaming
`seedlings.csv` to `seedlings.xlsx` does not make an Excel file, and Excel
refuses to open it because the contents are still plain text. Changing a format
needs a program that rewrites the file, such as **Save As** with another format.

## A practice copy of the measurements

The files in `data` stay exactly as supplied, so that you can always start again
from what was measured. Copy `data/seedlings.csv` into `output` and rename the
copy `seedlings-practice.csv`, checking that the name still ends in `.csv`. Open
the copy in a spreadsheet program to see the same 24 plants as a table, then
close it without saving. Tomorrow's exercises use this copy.

## Your first plain-text note

Create a new plain-text file in the text editor (on Mac, **Format → Make Plain
Text**) and write a few sentences: what one row of `data/seedlings.csv`
describes and in which units, one thing an `.xlsx` file can store that a `.csv`
file cannot, and why raw data should not be saved from a spreadsheet. Use
**Save As** to save it as `day01-notes.txt` in `reports`, and check in the file
manager that the name ends in `.txt` and not `.txt.txt` or `.rtf`. Then close
the editor, go to `reports` in the file manager and open the note again to
check that your last sentence was saved.

## Which files in the course folder are plain text?

Open each file in the text editor to find out which files in the course folder
R could read directly. Check every file in `data` and in `examples`, and
`report.Rmd`, `introcomputing.Rproj` and `START-HERE.txt` in the project folder,
without changing or saving any of them. Write the result in a new plain-text
file `reports/file-types.txt`, one line per file, with the kind of program meant
to open each file that is not plain text:

```text
data/seedlings.csv       plain text   table, commas between values
examples/seedlings.xlsx  not text     spreadsheet program (ZIP package)
```

If a file shows only readable words and numbers, it is plain text; if it starts
with `PK`, `%PDF` or `PNG` and then unreadable symbols, it is not.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your list

Plain text: every file in `data`, `report.Rmd`, `introcomputing.Rproj` (a few
RStudio settings written as text), `START-HERE.txt`, and in `examples` the files
`README.txt`, `seedling-notes.txt`, `genes.csv` and `seedlings-semicolon.csv`.
Not plain text: `seedling-notes.docx` (word processor), `seedlings.xlsx`
(spreadsheet), `seedling-notes.pdf` (PDF reader) and `seedlings-plot.png`
(image viewer).
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## You open a `.docx` file in Notepad and see `PK` and strange symbols. Is the file broken?

No. A `.docx` is a compressed ZIP package of XML files, so Notepad shows its raw
bytes, while Word unpacks the package and shows the formatted document.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A colleague sends a gene list as `.xlsx` and `MARCH1` appears as `1-Mar`. What happened?

A spreadsheet converted the gene symbol to a date when the list was opened and
saved, and the name cannot be recovered from the date. Ask for the original file.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## You rename `seedlings-practice.csv` to `seedlings-practice.txt`. What changed?

Only the name. The file still holds the same commas and numbers, and a text
editor shows the same contents.
:::

**Save today:** `reports/day01-notes.txt`, `reports/file-types.txt` and
`output/seedlings-practice.csv`.
